free_text_drill: No sloppy reps; guard stays up
Where did you hit your 40% wall?
Who represented the gym well today?

• Jump rope: 2 minutes continuous
• Shadow boxing: 2 rounds × 90 seconds

• Mirror drills: Partners mirror footwork without contact
• Distance management: Maintain range while moving

• Jab-cross on mitts: Focus on form
• Defensive reflexes: Slip, roll, parry at 30% speed
WATCH FOR
• Proper warm-up intensity (gradual increase)
• Full range of motion in shoulders and hips
• Athletes maintaining balance during movement

Review Today's Focus Points:
1. Distance control: Maintaining optimal range
2. Defensive positioning: Hands up, chin down, elbows in
3. Combination structure: Entry punch → body work → exit

Structure: 3 rounds × 3 minutes with 1-minute rest
Athlete A - Offense (40%): Execute combinations on moving target. Focus on distance and accuracy. Reset after each combination.
Athlete B - Defense: Maintain guard and footwork. Slip, parry, or move - NO COUNTERS. Communicate if contact too heavy.
COACHING CUES
"Control distance before you punch" • "Defender keep moving" • "Touch don't push - land clean, pull back" • "Reset to neutral"
SAFETY
Stop if frustration shown • Verify 40% power • Mix head and body targets

Progression: Defender may now counter (50% contact)
Athlete A - Offense: Same combination work. React to counters defensively. Expect return fire.
Athlete B - Defense + Counter: Single shots only (jab or cross). No combinations - single punch and reset. Focus on timing not power.
COACHING CUES
"Offense - defend the counter before reset" • "Defense - one clean counter, then out" • "Control and communicate" • "If too much say 'break'"
WATCH FOR
Power escalation - reset if heavy • Hands dropping after punching • Loss of technique under pressure

Final Progression: Controlled free exchange at 60% contact. Athletes punch and counter while maintaining defense. Work in 3-4 punch bursts, reset every 20-30 seconds.
Coach Control: Call "time" every 30 seconds. Stop if technique breaks down. Rotate partners after each 3-minute round.
COACHING CUES
"Work smart, not hard - technique first" • "Break!" - immediate reset • "Breathe between exchanges" • "Hands up after you punch"
CRITICAL SAFETY
No headhunting or targeting one area repeatedly. Stop on any sign of ego or emotion. Touch gloves before and after rounds. Coach has absolute authority to stop or reduce intensity.
Open Sparring: 3 rounds × 3 minutes, 1-minute rest. Athletes choose partners (coach approval). Previous rules apply, intensity capped at 70%. Coach provides active supervision.

Cool-Down: Light movement and stretching (2 min), deep breathing (1 min).
Debrief: Discuss what worked and needs improvement. Individual check-ins for concerns or injuries. Reinforce safety culture and respect.
POST-SESSION WATCH: Check for delayed injury signs. Document incidents. Note athletes needing additional safety coaching.

free_text_drill:
Time: 2–3 minutes
Purpose
Before movement starts, the athlete should assess their current state. This creates awareness and helps regulate the session.
Directions
Stand tall and relaxed. Take a few normal breaths. Notice:
how the shoulders feel
whether the neck feels tight
how easy it is to raise the hands to guard
whether the hips feel loose or stiff
whether the feet feel springy or heavy
whether the mind feels calm or rushed
Do not judge the body. Just observe it.
What to notice
soreness
heaviness
asymmetry
tight breathing
elevated shoulders
stiff upper back
tired legs
Teaching point
Active recovery starts with awareness. If the athlete never learns to feel their condition, they will always train the same way regardless of what their body is telling them.

free_text_drill:
Time: 8–10 minutes
This section prepares the body without creating stress.
A. Neck mobility
Time: 1 minute
Purpose
Hard punching and guard position often create neck and upper trap tension. Gentle neck movement helps reduce stiffness.
Directions
Stand relaxed. Slowly tilt the head:
down slightly
back to neutral
ear toward left shoulder
back to neutral
ear toward right shoulder
back to neutral
Then slowly turn the head left and right.
Keep all movements small and comfortable. No aggressive stretching.
What it should feel like
A release of stiffness, not a stretch battle.
Common mistakes
forcing range
rolling the neck too aggressively
shrugging the shoulders while moving the head
B. Shoulder rolls
Time: 1 minute
Purpose
Boxing heavily involves the shoulders. Rolls help restore motion in the shoulder girdle and reduce trapped tension.
Directions
Lift both shoulders up, roll them backward, then let them drop. Repeat for several slow reps. Then reverse direction.
Move deliberately, not fast.
What to feel
shoulder blades gliding
neck softening
chest opening slightly
tension leaving the traps
Teaching point
Many athletes think shoulders are supposed to stay “on” all the time. Recovery teaches that relaxed shoulders are often faster and healthier shoulders.
C. Arm circles
Time: 1–2 minutes
Purpose
To warm the shoulder joint through controlled motion and improve circulation to the upper body.
Directions
Extend the arms lightly out to the side or slightly forward. Make:
small circles
medium circles
large circles
Do forward circles first, then backward.
Stay smooth. Do not turn it into a burn challenge.
What to feel
Gradual warmth through the shoulder, upper arm, and upper back.
Common mistakes
doing too many too fast
tensing the fists
lifting the shoulders toward the ears
D. Torso rotations
Time: 1–2 minutes
Purpose
Punching uses rotational mechanics. After a hard day, the trunk can feel rigid. Rotations restore fluidity.
Directions
Stand with feet under the hips or in a light stance. Keep knees soft. Rotate the torso left and right in a relaxed rhythm. Let the arms stay loose.
You are not trying to crank the spine. You are letting the trunk unwind.
What to feel
the ribcage moving
the spine loosening
the hips softly following
easier turning from side to side
Common mistakes
twisting too hard
locking the knees
trying to make it dramatic
E. Scapular reach and retract
Time: 1 minute
Purpose
Punching requires the shoulder blade to move well. This drill restores scapular rhythm.
Directions
Bring the hands up in front as if lightly touching an invisible wall. Reach the arms forward slightly by letting the shoulder blades glide around the ribcage. Then gently pull the shoulder blades back without arching the lower back.
Repeat slowly.
What to feel
Movement around the upper back, not just the arms.
Teaching point
A lot of shoulder discomfort in boxing comes from the athlete thinking only about the arm and forgetting the shoulder blade.
F. Hip and stance loosen-up
Time: 1–2 minutes
Purpose
Even if yesterday’s session focused on upper body work, a boxer still needs hip freedom and stance comfort.
Directions
Stand in stance and lightly shift weight:
front foot to back foot
left to right
small pivots
gentle step-ins and step-outs
Everything should feel light.
What to feel
feet reconnecting with the floor
hips becoming less sticky
stance becoming natural again

Time: 3–4 minutes
Purpose
This transitions the body from general movement into boxing-specific recovery movement.
Directions
Get into stance and move lightly:
bounce gently on the balls of the feet
shift forward and back
step left and right
pivot softly
maintain relaxed guard
No hard punching yet.
The goal is to feel athletic without effort.
What it should feel like
springy
relaxed
balanced
calm
controlled
Breathing
Breathe normally through the nose as much as possible. Do not hold the breath.
Common mistakes
stomping
over-bouncing
tensing the calves
raising the shoulders
treating it like conditioning footwork
Teaching point
A good boxing stance should feel alive, not rigid. Recovery days are a great time to rediscover that.

free_text_drill:
Time: 3 rounds of 2 minutes, 1 minute easy rest between rounds
This is the heart of the session.
The athlete is not using shadowboxing here to test toughness or get tired. They are using it to restore clean boxing.
ROUND 1 — FORM ROUND
Purpose
To re-groove the basic punches with perfect mechanics and minimal effort.
Directions
Throw simple punches at about 40–50% speed and very low power:
jab
cross
jab-cross
single rear hand
jab to guard return
cross to guard return
If you want to add hooks or uppercuts, keep them slow and short.
Between combinations, pause just enough to confirm your position:
feet under you
hands back home
chin controlled
shoulders relaxed
Main focus points
straight punches go straight out and straight back
hands return immediately to guard
shoulders stay relaxed
no lunging
no pushing the air
no forcing speed
What it should feel like
Like practicing in front of a coach who only cares about clean mechanics.
Common mistakes
going too fast because shadowboxing feels too easy
letting the punches drift long
dropping the rear hand
leaning too far into the jab
punching with tension
Coaching cues
“Touch and return”
“Long spine, relaxed shoulders”
“Clean line, clean recovery”
“Demo-level form”
Teaching point
This round teaches a major recovery lesson: sometimes the body heals best when you rehearse skill with low cost.
ROUND 2 — MOVEMENT ROUND
Purpose
To reconnect punching with footwork, balance, and spatial control.
Directions
Begin moving lightly in stance. Add:
step and jab
step back and reset
small pivots
step left or right with light punches
angle out after a 1–2
soft rhythm changes
Keep all movement under control. The feet should feel organized, not busy.
Punch volume should stay low to moderate. The focus is the quality of moving while boxing.
Main focus points
never cross the feet
keep the base under the body
move first when appropriate, punch second
finish every action balanced
let the feet carry the punches, not the other way around
What it should feel like
The body should feel like it is gliding, not grinding.
Common mistakes
bouncing too much
moving without purpose
reaching with punches instead of stepping correctly
rushing transitions
getting sloppy because there is no target
Coaching cues
“Glide, don’t stomp”
“Feet set the table”
“Move quiet”
“Always land in balance”
Teaching point
When fighters are fatigued, footwork usually gets messy before they realize it. Recovery days are ideal for restoring movement discipline.
ROUND 3 — FLOW ROUND
Purpose
To rebuild rhythm, looseness, and boxing IQ under very light conditions.
Directions
Move freely and mix:
straights
hooks
uppercuts
simple combinations
defensive exits
angle changes
guard recoveries
This is still light. The athlete should feel expressive, not forceful.
Use combinations like:
jab-cross
jab-jab-cross
cross-hook-cross
jab-hook-cross
uppercut-hook
jab-cross-roll
jab-step out
cross-hook-pivot out
Do not worry about winning the round. Worry about the flow of good boxing.
Main focus points
keep everything compact
maintain rhythm
stay relaxed through transitions
let defense happen naturally after offense
no chaotic flurries
What it should feel like
Smooth, fluid, and intelligent. Like boxing with no urgency.
Common mistakes
turning “flow” into random punching
throwing too many shots because there is no resistance
losing structure between combinations
forgetting defense after offense
Coaching cues
“Flow, don’t force”
“Stay smooth between phases”
“Every combo ends in position”
“Nothing wild”
Teaching point
Flow rounds help the athlete rediscover boxing timing without the emotional pressure of impact.

free_text_drill:
Time: 6–8 minutes
Defense is excellent for active recovery because it can sharpen perception and positioning without impact or muscular strain.
A. Slip drill
Time: 2 minutes
Purpose
To sharpen head movement and rhythm while keeping the body relaxed.
Directions
Imagine a straight punch coming at your face. Slip slightly to one side, return to center, then slip to the other side.
Keep the movement small. It is a clean angle change, not a dramatic bend.
Hands stay near guard. Eyes forward.
What to feel
neck relaxed
knees soft
trunk subtly engaged
movement coming from the whole body, not just the head
Common mistakes
moving too far
bending at the waist
taking the eyes off the line
turning the slip into a squat
Cue
“Just enough to miss.”
B. Roll under drill
Time: 2 minutes
Purpose
To restore coordinated defensive movement under the base.
Directions
Imagine a hook coming. Bend the knees slightly, rotate under the imaginary punch, and come up on the other side in balance.
Move left and right.
Keep the spine organized. The torso rotates with the legs.
What to feel
legs supporting the movement
hips and trunk working together
head staying controlled
easy return to stance
Common mistakes
folding forward
making the roll too deep
losing stance width
coming up out of balance
Cue
“Under control, under the shot, back to stance.”
C. Pull-back drill
Time: 1–2 minutes
Purpose
To rehearse distance management and controlled rearward movement.
Directions
From stance, slightly draw the head and upper body back as if avoiding a jab or cross. Then return to position.
You can add a light counter jab or cross afterward, but only if it remains smooth and easy.
What to feel
balance remains centered
the movement is small and efficient
no panic or overreaction
Common mistakes
leaning too far
straightening the whole body stiffly
falling onto the back leg
losing readiness to return
Cue
“Small escape, fast return.”
D. Defense into reset
Time: 1–2 minutes
Purpose
To teach the boxer to reconnect defense with composure.
Directions
Combine light defensive motions:
slip-slip
roll-roll
pull-reset
slip-counter-reset
roll-step out
Everything ends with a calm, balanced return to stance.
Teaching point
Recovery is not just physical. It is also the restoration of organized movement after action.

free_text_drill:
Time: 8–10 minutes
This section is especially important after a weighted punching day.
A. Wall slides
Sets/Reps: 2 sets of 8–12 slow reps
Purpose
To restore shoulder mobility, upward rotation mechanics, and posture control.
Directions
Stand with your back against a wall if possible. Bring the arms into a goalpost or bent-arm position. Slowly slide the arms upward, then back down, while keeping the ribcage controlled.
Only go through the range you can control.
What to feel
upper back working gently
shoulder blades moving
shoulders opening without strain
Common mistakes
arching the lower back
shrugging excessively
forcing the arms higher than control allows
Teaching point
Good shoulder mechanics are not just about “mobility”; they are about controlled movement of the shoulder blade and ribcage together.
B. Scapular push-ups
Sets/Reps: 2 sets of 8–10 reps
Purpose
To improve scapular control and restore healthy shoulder function for punching.
Directions
Get into a push-up position against a wall, bench, or floor depending on comfort. Keep the elbows straight. Let the chest sink slightly between the shoulders, then press the floor or wall away so the shoulder blades spread apart.
Only the shoulder blades move. The elbows stay straight.
What to feel
work around the shoulder blades
light activation through serratus and upper trunk
no neck tension
Common mistakes
bending the elbows
rushing the reps
shrugging
collapsing the core
Cue
“Glide in, glide out.”
C. Band pull-aparts if a band is available
Sets/Reps: 2 sets of 12–15
Purpose
To bring some balance to the upper body after repeated forward punching actions.
Directions
Hold a light band at chest height with straight but not locked arms. Pull the band apart by moving the hands outward while keeping the ribcage stacked and the neck relaxed. Return under control.
What to feel
upper back activation
shoulder blades drawing together smoothly
chest staying relaxed
Common mistakes
lifting the shoulders
using a band that is too strong
arching the lower back
jerking the band apart
Cue
“Open the chest without tensing the neck.”
D. Arm shake-outs
Time: 30–60 seconds between exercises
Purpose
To release accumulated tension.
Directions
Let the arms hang and shake them loosely. Relax the hands, elbows, and shoulders.
Teaching point
Boxers often underestimate how much low-level tension they carry after training. Shake-outs teach active relaxation.

Purpose
To extend circulation work, support recovery, and help the athlete mentally downshift.
Good choices

free_text_drill:
Time: 3–5 minutes
This is a major part of the session, not an afterthought.
Purpose
To reduce tension, downshift the nervous system, and help the body move from training mode into recovery mode.
Directions
Sit, stand, or lie down comfortably. Place one or both hands on the ribs or lower ribcage.
Breathe in through the nose for about 4 seconds.
Exhale slowly through the mouth for about 6 to 8 seconds.
Do not force giant breaths. Let the breath be smooth.
Repeat for several cycles.
What to feel
heart rate settling
shoulders dropping
jaw softening
body becoming quieter
mind becoming less hurried
Common mistakes
trying to breathe too deeply
lifting the shoulders while inhaling
rushing the exhale
turning it into performance breathing
Teaching point
The end of a recovery session should feel like the body is being taught to relax on purpose, not just told to relax.
